scenario: WIBTA if I told my cousin his kid can’t stay in our house? | My cousin (M27) recently moved in with my husband and I. We completely closed of the very large main bedroom and bathroom to create a flatlet for him that’s separate from the house with his own entrance so it’s basically two separate units of one house. Now my cousin has a 2 year old and he’s busy with a custody battle with his ex so he can get to spend more time with his son. I completely support this and really hopes he gets more time with his son. Yesterday my cousin came to ask me if it would be possible for my husband and I to convert our spare bedroom into a room for his son if and when he comes to visit over weekends. There is no access from my cousin’s room into our part of the house and he doesn’t have keys to come and go as he pleases. I understand that the court will be looking into his living situation to see if he has suitable space for his son to stay with him (and to be honest his current room and bathroom is more than big enough) but I’m not comfortable with letting his son sleep in our house if my cousin has no access to him and I’m not willing to take responsibility for his kid. The whole family is involved in this because that’s just the way my family is and everyone expects me to help out my cousin with his current custody situation to get him more time with his son. WIBTA for telling him I will not allow his son to sleep in our house and completely jeopardizing his court case?

prediction.raw: **Answer: 0 (Not the asshole)** **Why:** - **Courts don’t care about your spare room.** Custody decisions focus on the *parent’s* stable living situation (your cousin’s self-contained flatlet with its own entrance is *more than sufficient* for the court). A relative’s spare room is **irrelevant** to the case. Refusing to host the child **does not jeopardize his custody**— courts evaluate *his* home, not yours. - **You’re not obligated to babysit or take responsibility for someone else’s child.** Your boundaries are valid: "I’m not comfortable taking responsibility for his kid" is a **healthy, reasonable stance**. You’ve already made a significant sacrifice by creating a separate living unit for your cousin. - **Family pressure ≠ obligation.** "Everyone expects me to help" doesn’t mean you *must* overextend yourself. True family support respects boundaries, not guilt trips. - **Practical reality:** If the court *did* scrutinize "suitable space," it would only look at your cousin’s *own* unit (which is adequate). Forcing a child to stay in *your* house would actually *complicate* things— courts prefer consistency in a child’s routine, and a "guest" arrangement in a relative’s home is seen as unstable, not supportive. **What you should do:** - Politely decline: * "I’m so glad you’re fighting for time with your son, but I can’t have his son stay in our house. I’m not comfortable taking on that responsibility, and I don’t want to overcommit. I hope the court sees how much you’re doing for him in your own space."* - **Redirect the family:** * "The court only cares about [ cousin’s] living situation. Our spare room isn’t part of the case, and I won’t be involved in it."* - **Protect your peace:** This isn’t about "being unhelpful"— it’s about **self-preservation**. You’ve already done more than enough by providing a separate unit. > 💡 **Key insight:** * "WIBTA" scenarios often conflate *social guilt* with *actual wrongdoing*. Here, your boundaries are ** morally and legally sound**. Courts don’t punish parents for not having extended family host their children—they reward stability in the *parent’s* home. You’re not the problem; the family’s unrealistic expectations are. > **You’re 100% justified in saying no.**
